passage: The ball rolled under the bench in the school yard in Lyon, and Selin grabbed it before Nour could. "Mine first!" Selin sang, the same way she had sung it all week. Nour shoved her shoulder, hard. Selin sat down on the gravel and her knee went red. When Madame Aubert hurried over, Nour's arms were folded tight. "She was being annoying. She always takes the ball and sings that silly song. She made me do it." Madame Aubert crouched beside Selin first and checked the knee, then looked up at Nour. "Singing is one thing. Pushing is another. Whose hands pushed?" Nour stared at the gravel and kicked a small stone. "Mine," she said at last, very quietly.

qa.q: What did Nour do when Selin grabbed the ball first?
qa.a: Nour shoved her shoulder, hard, and Selin sat down on the gravel with a red knee.

qa.q: Why did it feel fair to Nour to say Selin made her do it?
qa.a: After a whole week of the song, Nour was cross, so calling Selin annoying made the push feel like Selin's fault rather than Nour's own choice.

qa.q: At what moment could Nour have made a different choice, and what could it have been?
qa.a: Right when Selin sang "Mine first!", Nour could have walked away or told Madame Aubert about the ball-grabbing instead of using her hands.

qa.q: How might Selin feel hearing Nour say she made her do it?
qa.a: Sitting there with a sore knee, Selin may feel hurt twice: once by the push and again by being blamed for it 😢.

grounding: Shows a child turning the classmate she pushed into the cause of the push, so her own action feels justified.

passage: At the swimming club, the queue for the diving board was long. Ishita kept splashing water at the boys waiting behind her and laughing. When her turn came, Naveen gave her a push from behind, and she slapped into the water sideways, coughing. The coach blew the whistle and sent Naveen to the bench. Suraj sat down next to him, dripping. "Why'd you do that?" "She was being so irritating, yaar. Splash, splash, splash. She had it coming." Naveen kept his eyes on the pool. "If she'd just stood quietly, nothing would have happened." Suraj watched Ishita climb out, rubbing her ear. "She splashed. You pushed," he said. Naveen didn't answer, but he stopped swinging his legs.

qa.q: Where did Naveen push Ishita?
qa.a: At the swimming club, from behind in the diving-board queue, so she slapped into the water sideways, coughing.

qa.q: What does Naveen's line "If she'd just stood quietly" suggest about how he sees the push?
qa.a: It suggests Naveen feels defensive, blaming Ishita's splashing so he can believe he only reacted and did nothing really wrong.

qa.q: What choice could Naveen have made when the splashing started?
qa.a: He could have told Ishita to stop, moved further back in the queue, or called the coach instead of pushing.

qa.q: How does Suraj see the push differently from Naveen?
qa.a: Suraj separates the two acts: Ishita splashed, but Naveen chose to push, so the push is Naveen's to own.

grounding: Shows a boy justifying a push by insisting the irritating girl brought it on herself.

passage: I'm Sunaina, and I sit two benches behind Vikas in Class 5. On Tuesday, Pallavi kept tapping her ruler on his desk all through drawing period, tap, tap, tap. At break, near the water cooler, Vikas pushed her and she dropped her steel bottle. It rolled all the way to the stairs. Later Vikas told our group, "She was irritating me the whole period. She deserved it." Some boys nodded. I don't know what was really going on inside him. He sounded sure, but he kept looking over at Pallavi, who was sitting alone on the steps. After lunch I saw him pick up her bottle from the stairs and leave it on her desk without saying a word.

subtype: Saying the target should have known better [Observer]
passage: So, you want the story I'm least proud of? Fine. I'm Damini, and in Class 10 my closest friend was Lalremsiami. Some girls in our section started giggling and copying her accent every time she answered in class. One evening she messaged me, "I don't want to go tomorrow." And I typed back, "Yaar, you're too sensitive. Just toughen up, ignore them." I remember feeling almost relieved after I sent it, like the problem was now hers to fix, not mine. She replied with one word: "ok." Next day she sat with her head down all through English. Honestly? Watching them tease her made my stomach twist, and telling her to be stronger was easier than standing next to her. It took me a month to say sorry.

qa.q: What did Damini type back when Lalremsiami said she didn't want to go tomorrow?
qa.a: Damini typed, "Yaar, you're too sensitive. Just toughen up, ignore them."

qa.a: When the "I don't want to go tomorrow" message came, Damini could have asked what was happening, offered to sit with her, and suggested telling a teacher together.

qa.q: What might the one-word reply "ok" tell us about Lalremsiami?
qa.a: It may show Lalremsiami felt shut down and alone, as if even her closest friend thought the teasing was her own fault 🥺.

passage: Parul, sit, let me tell you something since you're starting college. When I was a young man of twenty, I got a letter saying I'd won a scooter in a lucky draw. Just pay a small "delivery fee" by money order, it said. I sent almost my whole month's hostel money. No scooter came, of course. When I told my elder brother, he laughed and said, "Harish, you're a fool. Who wins scooters? You deserved to lose it." I didn't eat properly for days, not from hunger but from shame. It was my roommate Jacob who sat with me, said, "They're thieves, you're not stupid," and walked with me to the post office and the police chowki to report it. The money never came back. But the shame slowly left.

qa.q: What did Harish's elder brother say when he heard about the lost money?
qa.a: He laughed and said, "Harish, you're a fool. Who wins scooters? You deserved to lose it."

qa.a: Jacob named the cheats as the thieves and then walked with Harish to the post office and the police chowki, so listening came with real steps.

qa.q: How might things have gone if the elder brother had reacted the way Jacob did?
qa.a: Harish would likely have felt less alone and ashamed, and might not have spent days hardly eating.

grounding: An elder recalls being told a scam was his own fault, and how a friend's listening and practical help eased the shame.

You basically handed it over," he said, and hung up to take another call. She sat on the stairs with her face hot, thinking maybe he was right, maybe she was just gullible. Bhupen, from the next room, came down with a torch and a power bank. He listened to the whole thing without interrupting. Then he said, "Plug in. First, the bank's card-block number. Then we file it on the cybercrime portal before the battery dies." They finished the complaint at 11:40 by torchlight.

passage:
'Did you hear about Rupa and that manager?' Jasleen asked her sister, drying the steel plates.
'Mm. Mausi told me.' Alka shook her head. 'But why did she keep going to those late meetings? Why did she let it go on for months?' She stopped, a plate in her hand. 'Wait. Listen to me.'
'What?'
'I'm asking what Rupa did wrong. She didn't make him send those messages at midnight. She didn't make him threaten her appraisal.'
Jasleen leaned on the counter. 'So what's the real question?'
'Who had the power there? He did. He chose to send them. He chose to hold her job over her head.'
Alka put the plate down. 'I'm calling Rupa tonight. Not to ask why. Just to ask how she's doing and what she needs.'
'I'll sit with you while you call,' Jasleen said.

qa.q: What did Alka say the manager chose to do?
qa.a: He chose to send the messages at midnight and chose to hold Rupa's job over her head.

qa.q: Why did Alka stop with a plate in her hand?
qa.a: She noticed that her questions were all about what Rupa did wrong, and it bothered her that she was blaming the person who was hurt.

qa.q: What did Alka decide once she changed her question?
qa.a: She decided to call Rupa that night just to ask how she was doing and what she needed, instead of asking why she let it go on.

qa.q: How might Rupa feel if the call began with 'why did you keep going to those meetings'?
qa.a: Rupa would probably feel judged and ashamed, and might stop telling her family anything about the manager.

grounding: A woman catches herself asking why Rupa let harassment continue and turns the question to who held power and chose to act.

passage: Last month my flatmate Jaya came home shaking; two men on a bike had snatched her phone outside the metro station. My first words, and I'm not proud of them, were, "Why were you holding it out on that road? You know that stretch." She went quiet and took her tea to her room. I'm Uma, and I've always thought of myself as the practical one. That night I lay awake replaying it. Jaya didn't grab her own phone and ride away with it. Two men planned it, waited for someone distracted, and chose to do it. My question had quietly put her on trial. The next morning I knocked, sat on her floor, and said, "I'm sorry. They did this, not you." Then I helped her fill in the police complaint.

qa.q: What happened to Jaya outside the metro station?
qa.a: Two men on a bike snatched her phone outside the metro station.

qa.q: Why did Uma lie awake that night replaying the conversation?
qa.a: Uma felt uneasy that the first question had put Jaya on trial instead of the two men, which clashed with how Uma wanted to treat a friend.

qa.a: Uma apologised, told Jaya "They did this, not you," and helped with the police complaint, taking the blame off Jaya and giving practical help.

qa.a: Jaya probably felt hurt and blamed, as if coming home shaken wasn't enough and she also had to defend herself 🥺.

passage: Supervisor's note, Thursday. At today's shift review, Samir, our newest team lead, went through Tuesday's incident, when a delivery contractor shouted at Francis and shoved a crate at him. Samir began, "Why did Francis let it get that far? He could have walked off." Then he paused, looked at his notes, and said, "Actually, that's the wrong question. The contractor chose to shout. The contractor chose to shove the crate. What do we do about that?" The room shifted. Francis, who had kept his eyes on the table, looked up. The team agreed the contractor's firm will be informed, and loading will now have two staff present. Afterwards I thanked Samir for correcting himself in front of everyone. I also checked in with Francis privately; he said he felt heard. R. Kulkarni, shift supervisor

passage: At the photocopy shop outside the government college in Hanumangarh, Bhavna counted out notes and slid them across to the man at the counter. "Project file, commerce, final year. Handwritten, please." Her cousin Kunal, who worked the binding machine in the back, looked up. On the bus home Kunal asked quietly, "You're buying the whole project?" Bhavna stared out at the mustard fields. "Everyone does it. In the city, people buy whole degrees with a seal and signature. I'm only buying one file." "You topped the district in Class 12," Kunal said. "You didn't need anyone then." Bhavna shifted her dupatta and didn't answer. The receipt stayed folded small in her fist.

qa.q: What did Bhavna ask the man at the counter for?
qa.a: A project file for final-year commerce, handwritten.

qa.q: Why does "I'm only buying one file" seem reasonable to Bhavna?
qa.a: She sets the bar at city people buying whole degrees, so one bought project looks small and her unease can be pushed away.

qa.q: What choice is still open to Bhavna with the receipt in her fist?
qa.a: She could go back, cancel the order, and ask a teacher or Kunal to help her plan the project in the time left.

qa.q: What might Kunal be feeling on the bus?
qa.a: Kunal seems disappointed and worried, remembering a cousin who topped the district without help and is now paying for someone else's work.

grounding: A small-town student justifies buying a project file because others buy whole degrees.

subtype: Cutting corners because the rest do worse [Actor]
passage: It was past midnight in their shared apartment in Toronto when Kaito saw the payment confirmation on Sami's laptop: "Order 4471, Data Structures Assignment 3, delivered by Thursday." "You paid someone to do your code?" Kaito asked. Sami rubbed his eyes. "Look, there are guys back home who bought a whole engineering degree. Stamped and everything. I'm buying one assignment out of twelve. It's basically nothing." "You're not them, though," Kaito said. "You're the one who wanted to build apps for your mum's bakery." Sami closed the laptop halfway. "That was before three part-time jobs." He sat there, not opening it again, not closing it either.

qa.q: What did Kaito see on Sami's laptop?
qa.a: A payment confirmation: "Order 4471, Data Structures Assignment 3, delivered by Thursday."

qa.q: Why does Sami call one bought assignment "basically nothing"?
qa.a: Sami is exhausted and defensive, so measured against guys who bought a whole engineering degree, one of twelve assignments looks tiny, and three part-time jobs feel like an excuse.

qa.q: What could Sami do while the laptop is still half open?
qa.a: He could ask whether the Sami who wanted to build apps for his mum's bakery would be okay with it, then talk to the course staff about his workload.

qa.q: Why might Kaito measure Sami differently than Sami does?
qa.a: Kaito compares Sami with Sami's own goals, not with strangers who cheated, so the bought code looks like a step away from who Sami wants to be.

grounding: A student abroad calls a ghostwritten assignment basically nothing because others bought whole degrees.

passage: At 7 p.m. in the Whitefield office, Mridul was filling in the travel claim from the Hyderabad trip. The client dinner had cost 1,800, but his own dinner the night before, 900, had no receipt and wasn't claimable. He hovered over the form. People in sales claimed taxi rides they never took; everyone knew it. A dinner was nothing. Then he pictured Sumit, who sat across from him and trusted his numbers on every shared project, scrolling through this claim. Would he be fine with Sumit reading line four? He deleted the line. When Sumit leaned over and asked, "Heading out?", Mridul said, "Yeah. Just finished the claim," and felt oddly light walking to the lift.

qa.q: Which dinner had no receipt?
qa.a: His own dinner the night before, 900, had no receipt.

qa.q: Why did adding the dinner feel almost acceptable to Mridul at first?
qa.a: At first Mridul felt at ease, comparing it with people in sales claiming taxi rides they never took, so one dinner seemed like nothing.

qa.q: What question helped Mridul decide, and why did it work?
qa.a: He asked whether he'd be fine with Sumit reading line four, which measured the claim by his own standard instead of by what others get away with.

qa.q: How might Sumit's trust be affected if the dinner had stayed in?
qa.a: Sumit relies on Mridul's numbers on every shared project; a padded claim, even unseen, would make that trust less deserved.

grounding: An office worker resists padding an expense claim by imagining a trusted colleague reading it.

passage:
'Mumma, what's that?' Minakshi asked, climbing onto the chair beside the laptop, crayon still in hand.
'My office expense form, baby. The money I spent on work.'
Sharmila's husband Deepak called from the sofa, 'Add the Pune hotel upgrade too. Your manager won't check. Everyone in your office pads a bit.'
'The upgrade was for me, not for work,' Sharmila said.
'So? Others claim whole family trips.'
Minakshi pointed at the screen. 'Can I read it? I know my numbers!'
Sharmila looked at the little finger on the screen. 'Would I read this line out to her?' she said softly.
'What?' said Deepak.
'Nothing. Just, no. If Minakshi can read it out loud and I don't wince, it goes in. The upgrade stays out.'
She deleted the line. 'Now you can read, baby.'

qa.q: What did Deepak tell Sharmila to add to the form?
qa.a: He told her to add the Pune hotel upgrade too.

qa.q: What was Sharmila thinking when she looked at Minakshi's finger on the screen?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and was wondering whether she could read the upgrade line out to her daughter without wincing, a quiet check against her own standard.

qa.q: What rule did Sharmila choose, and why is it hard to argue with?
qa.a: Anything Minakshi can read out loud without Sharmila wincing goes in; it measures the form by her own values, not by the family trips others claim.

qa.q: Why might Deepak see the upgrade differently from Sharmila?
qa.a: Deepak measures it against what others in the office get away with, so padding a bit looks normal to him, while Sharmila measures it against herself.

grounding: A mother tempted to pad an expense form asks whether she would be comfortable with her child reading it.

passage: I'm Tanvir, and last quarter I almost did something small and stupid. I'd lost the receipt for a site-visit lunch in Nashik, and the claim form let me type any amount. My team lead once told me, laughing, that someone in finance had claimed a whole wedding as "client entertainment." Next to that, rounding my lunch up to 1,200 felt like a rounding error. My cursor sat there for a while. Then I thought of Damini, who has worked beside me for two years and double-checks my reports because she knows I hate mistakes. If she opened this form, would I want to explain that number? I typed the real amount, 640, and attached a note about the lost receipt. Honestly, it felt better than the extra money would have.

qa.q: What amount did Tanvir finally type?
qa.a: The real amount, 640, with a note about the lost receipt.

qa.q: Why did rounding up to 1,200 feel like a rounding error to Tanvir at first?
qa.a: Tanvir felt tempted but not guilty, because beside the story of someone claiming a whole wedding, a padded lunch looked tiny and didn't feel like real dishonesty.

qa.q: Which question changed Tanvir's decision, and why does it work?
qa.a: Imagining Damini opening the form and asking "would I want to explain that number?" works because it uses a trusted person's eyes, not the worst example.

qa.q: How might Damini feel if she found a padded number in Tanvir's form?
qa.a: Damini, who double-checks Tanvir's reports out of care, might feel let down and start wondering what else needs checking.

grounding: The narrator avoids inflating a lunch claim by imagining a trusted colleague reading it.

passage: I'm Dilnaz, Zeenat's older sister. On Sunday I heard a crash from the balcony and found Ammi's clay flowerpot in pieces and Zeenat holding a skipping rope. When Ammi came, Zeenat said, "Billu jumped on the railing and knocked it." Billu is our neighbour's cat. By dinner she told the same story to Abbu, with more details: Billu's tail swishing, the pot wobbling. On Tuesday Nani asked, and Zeenat told it again, eyes wide, like she'd seen a film. Yesterday I said, "Zeenat, you were skipping there." She looked truly confused. "No, Dilnaz Api, I remember Billu." I don't know what's in her head. But she didn't look like she was lying anymore.

qa.q: What story did Zeenat tell Ammi about the flowerpot?
qa.a: "Billu jumped on the railing and knocked it."

qa.q: Why might Zeenat look truly confused when Dilnaz mentions the skipping?
qa.a: After telling the Billu story again and again with new details, it may now feel like a real memory to her, so Dilnaz's version sounds wrong.

qa.q: What choice could Ammi make that would make it easier for Zeenat to tell the truth?
qa.a: Ammi could calmly say the pot matters less than the truth and gently ask what Zeenat was doing on the balcony, so owning up feels safe.

qa.q: What is it like for Dilnaz to hear Zeenat insist she remembers Billu?
qa.a: Dilnaz is puzzled and a bit uneasy, having seen the skipping rope but unable to tell whether her sister is lying or truly believes it 🤔.

grounding: An older sister watches a younger girl's fib about the cat grow with retelling until it seems to become her memory.

passage:
Monday: Omkar hadn't done his maths homework. When Mrs Pillai asked, he said, "Ma'am, my notebook fell in a puddle on the way." Tushar, next to him, raised his eyebrows. Omkar kicked him under the desk.
Wednesday: At lunch, Omkar told the puddle story to the boys from the other section, adding a speeding auto that splashed him. He even showed how he'd tried to dry the pages under the fan.
Next Monday: Tushar said, "You know you just didn't do it, right?" Omkar frowned, really annoyed. "I did do it! It got wet, the auto splashed me. I remember my socks were soaked." Tushar opened his mouth, then shut it. Omkar sounded completely sure.

qa.q: What did Omkar tell Mrs Pillai happened to his notebook?
qa.a: He said, "Ma'am, my notebook fell in a puddle on the way."

qa.q: Why does Omkar sound completely sure by the next Monday?
qa.a: Each retelling added details like the auto and the soaked socks, so the made-up story now feels like something he truly remembers.

qa.q: At which point could Omkar have stopped the story from growing, and how?
qa.a: On the first Monday, when Tushar raised his eyebrows, he could have admitted he hadn't done it and asked Mrs Pillai for a day to finish.

qa.q: How does Tushar experience the conversation on the next Monday?
qa.a: Tushar knows the truth, so seeing his friend truly annoyed and certain leaves him puzzled and unsure whether to push further.

grounding: Across a week, a boy's homework excuse grows with retelling until he believes it himself.

passage: Suraj, come, sit. Your Wasim chacha will tell you something embarrassing. When I was ten, I lost my new cricket bat at the maidan; I simply forgot it under a tree. I was scared of Abba, so I said a tall boy from the next mohalla snatched it. Abba asked me once. Ammi asked me. My cousins asked me. Each time I told it, the tall boy got something new: a red cap, a scar on his chin, a bicycle. Years later, all grown up, I was chatting with my brother and described that red cap as if I'd seen it yesterday. Your abbu laughed and said, "Wasim, there was no boy. You told me under the tree that you'd forgotten it." I truly didn't believe him at first. That's how strong a repeated story is.

qa.q: Where did Wasim actually leave the new cricket bat?
qa.a: He simply forgot it under a tree at the maidan.

qa.q: Why did Wasim not believe his brother at first, years later?
qa.a: He had told the tall-boy story so many times, adding a red cap and a scar, that it felt like something he had actually seen.

qa.q: What small choice at ten could have kept the story from taking root?
qa.a: Telling Abba the first time that he'd forgotten the bat, even while scared, would have stopped the story before repeats made it feel real.

qa.q: How did Suraj's abbu see the old story differently from Wasim?
qa.a: Suraj's abbu remembered what was said under the tree, so to him the tall boy was just a made-up excuse, not a memory.

grounding: An uncle recalls how his childhood fib about a stolen bat became something he later believed he had seen.

passage:
Thursday: Sumit flipped through his biology notes on the metro, highlighter in hand. Photosynthesis, the diagram of the leaf, the chloroplast. All familiar. "I know this chapter cold," he texted Urmila. She replied, "Want me to quiz you?" "Nah, sorted 😎"
Saturday: Question 3 read, "Explain why a plant kept in the dark loses its green colour." Sumit stared. He could picture the page, even the yellow highlight, but not a single sentence of the answer.
Next Wednesday: The paper came back, 14 out of 40. Sumit read the number three times. "But I read everything," he said to Urmila at the bus stop. "Reading isn't the same as explaining," she said. "Tonight, close the book and tell me the leaf chapter."

qa.q: What mark did Sumit get when the paper came back?
qa.a: 14 out of 40.

qa.q: Why did Sumit feel so sure on Thursday that he knew the chapter?
qa.a: Sumit felt confident because every page looked familiar as he flipped through, so recognising the diagrams felt like understanding them.

qa.q: What turning point does Urmila offer Sumit, and why might it work?
qa.a: Closing the book and explaining the leaf chapter aloud shows what he truly knows, not just what looks familiar.

qa.q: How might Urmila have felt when Sumit turned down the quiz?
qa.a: Urmila may have suspected he was overconfident but let it go, and at the bus stop she chooses to help rather than say I told you so.

grounding: Over a week, a teenager mistakes familiar-looking notes for knowledge and is shocked by his mark.

passage: Santosh, you say you've "seen" all the chapters? Your Hansa ba said the same thing long ago. I was a girl of fifteen in Rajkot, in my Class 10 board year. The night before the history paper, I turned the pages of my notebook one by one, and each one felt like an old friend. The Mughal dates, the map of trade routes, all so familiar. I went to sleep smiling. Next morning the paper said, "Describe three causes of the revolt of 1857." I remembered exactly where the answer sat on the page, bottom left, underlined in red. But the causes? Gone. I sat for twenty minutes writing half-sentences. When the result came, I had barely passed, and I cried in the kitchen. My father didn't scold. He just said, "Next time, write it out without looking."

qa.q: What did Hansa ba remember about the answer to the 1857 question?
qa.a: She remembered exactly where the answer sat on the page, bottom left, underlined in red, but not the causes.

qa.q: Why did Hansa go to sleep smiling the night before the history paper?
qa.a: Every page felt like an old friend, so the familiarity made her believe she had truly learned it.

qa.q: What could Santosh try tonight instead of just turning pages?
qa.a: Santosh could shut the book and write the answers out without looking, as Hansa ba's father advised, to test what is really remembered.

qa.q: How might Santosh hear this story differently from a plain warning to study harder?
qa.a: Coming from Hansa ba's own memory of crying in the kitchen, it may feel real and kind to Santosh, and make that 'seen all the chapters' feeling look shakier 🙂.

grounding: A grandmother recalls how pages that felt familiar left her unable to answer, and she was shocked by the result.

passage: The power went out at 9 p.m., the night before the physics unit test, and Manjula's phone was already at thirty percent. No time to work through problems now. She lay on the bed with the torch on, scrolling through photos of Shreya's neat notes. Ohm's law, series circuits, the resistor diagrams. Each photo made her nod: yes, yes, done this. "Fully ready," she voice-noted Shreya before the battery died. In the test, the first numerical asked for the total resistance of a mixed circuit. The formula looked familiar, but she couldn't work out which one to use. Three days later: 9 out of 25. "But I knew it all," she whispered. Shreya, next to her, said, "You knew my notes. Want to solve ten problems with me this weekend?"

qa.q: What did Manjula scroll through by torchlight?
qa.a: Photos of Shreya's neat notes: Ohm's law, series circuits, the resistor diagrams.

qa.q: Why did Manjula feel "fully ready" after scrolling?
qa.a: Each photo looked familiar and made her nod, so seeing the ideas again felt like knowing how to use them.

qa.q: What choice does Shreya's weekend offer give Manjula?
qa.a: Solving ten problems together would test real understanding, so Manjula can find the gaps before the next test instead of after.

qa.q: What might Shreya be thinking when Manjula whispers "But I knew it all"?
qa.a: Shreya seems to see that Manjula recognised the notes without practising them, and wants to help rather than blame.

grounding: During a power cut, a teenager skims borrowed notes, feels ready, and is shocked by her mark.
